(1) the robustness of telecommunication networks is not related to their size, (2) the robustness is not related to the network structure, and (3) the robustness does not depend on the network topology.

(i) network robustness is a function of network size and degree distribution; (ii) network robustness can be improved by increasing the network size and the average degree; (iii) network robustness increases as the degree distribution becomes more uniform; and (iv) network robustness decreases when the network size increases.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the most important structural and centrality metrics for measuring the robustness of telecommunication networks experiencing failures are: (i) the network diameter, (ii) the average shortest path length, (iii) the average node connectivity, (iv) the average node betweenness centrality, and (v) the average node degree.
networks with similar topological properties have similar robustness.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the most robust networks are the ones with a high degree of clustering, low average shortest path length and a high average degree of nodes.
the networks which are more robust to multiple failures present a high number of links and nodes and are highly connected, which is a common feature of real telecommunication networks.
robustness is not a property which can be measured in isolation but rather it is the result of a set of topological properties which must be analyzed together in order to be fully understood.
The main takeaway from our work is that

network robustness is highly dependent on the multiple failures scenario considered, and the structural and centrality properties that are relevant for a particular scenario can be different from the ones relevant for another one.
the network topology has a significant impact on the robustness of a network.
robustness is a complex concept that cannot be measured with a single metric.
